name: Heavy compound lifting for testosterone
lead: Heavy compound lifting for testosterone refers to the practice of performing large multi-joint barbell exercises such as squats and deadlifts with the stated aim of raising testosterone levels, which proponents associate with a more masculine physique and appearance. The idea is common in fitness and looksmaxxing discussions of lifestyle ways to support testosterone.

Reference texts report that resistance training raises testosterone acutely, meaning a temporary rise around the time of the session, and that squats in particular produce acute increases in men [1][2]. The same texts note that this concerns short-term changes; they do not establish that these acute rises translate into durably higher baseline testosterone. Published sources reviewed for this entry did not include clinical trials testing that specific question.
infobox: Squat, deadlift and similar multi-joint lifts
Higher testosterone and a more muscular physique
Acute rises documented; long-term effect on baseline untested here

paras: Compound lifts recruit several large muscle groups at once. In the squat, the primary movers include the quadriceps, gluteus maximus, adductor magnus and soleus, with the trunk and hamstrings acting as stabilizers [2]. Proponents favour such lifts for testosterone because they involve a large amount of muscle mass.

Wikipedia's article on testosterone states that resistance training raises testosterone acutely, and that in older men protein intake may prevent that rise; it also states that endurance training in men may lower testosterone [1]. The article on the squat likewise reports acute increases in testosterone in men, together with acute rises in growth hormone and catecholamines, and notes that resistance-trained people have higher resting IGF-1 [2].

These sources describe hormone changes around exercise sessions. They do not, on their own, demonstrate that lifting heavy raises resting testosterone over months or years, or that any such change affects appearance beyond the muscle gained through training itself.

card.summary: Squats and deadlifts to push testosterone up; acute rises are documented, lasting baseline changes are not established in these sources.
card.note: Acute post-workout hormone rises are not the same as higher baseline testosterone.

quick.overview:
The idea is that heavy squats, deadlifts and other big barbell lifts raise testosterone, supporting a more muscular, masculine look. It is a common lifestyle approach in looksmaxxing circles.

Reference texts confirm short-term testosterone rises after resistance exercise. Whether this changes resting levels over time is not shown in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: Large multi-joint lifts engage a lot of muscle and produce acute hormone responses, including testosterone, growth hormone and catecholamines, around the session [2].
quick.risks: Lifting carries the usual training-related injury risks. No hormonal harms are described in the sources reviewed.
